one_liner: Schema-compiled binary format with generated C11, Go, Java and JavaScript code; beats protobuf-go and protobuf C++ 2-3x on small records.
what_it_does: Colfer is a binary format inspired by Protocol Buffers. Its compiler, colf, turns .colf schema files into plain source code for C (C11, usable from C++ through extern "C"), Go, Java and JavaScript. It is not a protobuf drop-in: it has its own IDL and its own wire format. Generated C gives one plain struct per type plus T_marshal_len(o), T_marshal(o, buf) and T_unmarshal(o, data, len), with errors reported through errno; generated Go gives MarshalTo, MarshalLen, MarshalBinary, Unmarshal and UnmarshalBinary methods.
how_it_is_fast: The compiler emits straight-line code specialized for each field, with no reflection, no descriptor tables and no runtime library. Fields must appear in schema order behind a 1-byte header (7-bit field index plus a flag), so unmarshal is one forward pass of `if (header == i)` checks, with no tag-dispatch loop and no unknown-field retention (unknown headers are rejected). Zero values are omitted, and the header flag picks a compact or fixed-width encoding per value (for example, a uint32 below 2^21 is a varint, larger values take 4 fixed big-endian bytes). T_marshal_len computes the exact size first, so marshal is a single pass into a preallocated buffer.
when_to_use: You control both ends and want one schema shared by C, Go, Java and JavaScript code, with no runtime library to link.

Hot paths with small, flat records (a few ints, floats and short strings): the project's C benchmark encodes a 7-field record in 9.19 ns and decodes it in 18.0 ns on an Apple M1, against 22.9 ns and 40.8 ns for protobuf C++.
Go services that can drop protobuf wire compatibility: 115/123 ns/op marshal/unmarshal against 287/356 ns/op for protobuf-go in the go_serialization_benchmarks SmallStruct test.

Untrusted network or stream input: the parser enforces a serial size cap (default 16 MiB) and a list length cap (default 64Ki), the C parser has an AFL round-trip fuzz harness, and each message ends in 0x7f, so messages can be concatenated.
C or embedded code that wants plain C11 structs from a code generator instead of linking libprotobuf.
when_not_to_use: You need protobuf wire compatibility, gRPC, reflection or dynamic messages, or a JSON mapping.
Rolling upgrades where old readers see data from newer writers: v1 readers reject fields they do not know. Forward compatibility exists only on the unreleased v2 branch.
Schemas that need maps, enums, integer lists, oneof, default values, or more than 127 fields per struct.

Read-mostly access to large messages: C unmarshal copies every string into its own malloc. In the same C benchmark, FlatBuffers reads the record in 6.69 ns against 18.0 ns for Colfer, though FlatBuffers is slower to build (62.4 ns).
Go-only hot paths that want the fastest codec: mus-go, benc and 200sc/bebop beat Colfer in the same harness, and gogo/protobuf ties it on marshal (115 ns/op).

integration.dependencies: None for generated code (C: libc only; Go: standard library only). The colf compiler is a Go program (prebuilt releases, go get, Homebrew, or a Maven plugin for Java). Its go.mod also pulls gogo/protobuf and flatbuffers, which its benchmarks use.
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler (CI builds with clang -std=c11 -pedantic -Werror; the benchmark uses -std=c17 and C++17); C++ uses the C header, and there is no C++ class API. Compiler module needs go 1.18. CI uses JDK 17 for Java.
integration.platforms: Any C11 target with 8-bit bytes (the header has #error otherwise), little- or big-endian (big-endian is detected by macros); Go, JVM/Android, Node.js/browsers.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Generated C functions keep no internal state, but they read the process-wide globals colfer_size_max and colfer_list_max and set errno.

gotchas: Unmarshal writes only the fields present in the serial. If you reuse a struct, absent fields keep stale values, so zero the struct first (C: calloc or memset; Go: *o = T{}). The Go benchmark harness does this. In C, an uninitialized .len field also makes marshal crash (issue #34).

C unmarshal mallocs every text, binary, list and nested struct. No free function is generated, malloc results are not checked for NULL, and a mid-message error leaves earlier allocations in the partial struct for the caller to free.

C T_marshal(o, buf) takes no buffer length. Size buf with T_marshal_len (it returns 0 and sets errno to EFBIG past the limits) or use colfer_size_max. The limits are global variables and the header guard is always COLFER_H, so each program gets one generated C pair. Go MarshalTo panics on a short buffer and fills nil entries of struct lists in the input.

Schema evolution is append-only: add new fields at the end and never remove fields (rename them to deprecate). C and Go do not validate UTF-8 in text fields. Java maps unsigned types to signed ones, and JavaScript 64-bit integers are limited to about 2^53.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Colfer over hpp-proto when you do not need protobuf wire compatibility and want the same schema in C, Go, Java and JavaScript; pick hpp-proto to stay protobuf-compatible in C++. In Go-only code, mus-go, benc and 200sc/bebop are faster in the same harness (214, 184 and 206 ns/op total against Colfer's 238), so choose Colfer for its C, Java and JavaScript generators and its parser size limits, not for raw Go speed.
verified_claims_summary: Go: the user-generated alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks report (no CPU model or Go version, last regenerated 2025-07-04) shows Colfer at 115 ns/op marshal and 123 ns/op unmarshal for the 6-field SmallStruct, against 287/356 ns/op for google.golang.org/protobuf v1.34.2 and 115/166 ns/op for gogo/protobuf v1.3.2. C: the project wiki reports c/bench/bench.cpp (Google Benchmark, -O3, Apple clang 15.0.0, Apple M1 iMac, libprotoc 24.4 generated C++ with no arena) at 9.19 vs 22.9 ns marshal (~2.5x) and 18.0 vs 40.8 ns unmarshal (~2.3x) for a 7-field record with one short string, from a single run with no variance given.
status_note: Activity is low: the last tagged release is v1.8.1 (2020-06-18), the last maintainer commit is from 2023-10, and community fixes were merged in 2025-11 and 2026-02. The v2 format (forward compatibility; a C preview at 5.63/13.3 ns) sits unreleased on a branch last touched 2024-01. The code is CC0 public domain with no patent grant, and the generated code is small enough to vendor.
